Josour for Windows and macOS · Phase 1 of 4 · for review

Desktop foundation and UI audit

The plan for rebuilding the desktop app (client/src/Josour.App, Avalonia 11.3) around the qantara mark, consistent with the phone that shipped in v2.6.0. This page covers what the app looks like today, an audit ranked by impact, the desktop tokens on top of the approved phone tokens, where the identity should live, and the icon plan for each system with rendered proofs. Nothing in the app has changed yet.

14 decisions I need from you before Phase 2 (answer each with yes, no or an alternative)
  1. One source of truth. A shared project, Josour.Brand, holds the tokens (both themes), Readex Pro, the logo geometry and the brand controls (lock-up, motif, icons) for both apps. One tokens file, docs/design/brand-tokens.json (today's mobile-tokens.json plus the desktop section), and one generator, scripts/brand-theme.py --check. The alternative is to extend mobile-theme.py to write a second Tokens.axaml into Josour.App. Cost and risk.
  2. Main window: layout A. A status hero is always at the top of the window, with the availability switch, above two tabs (Contacts, This device), at 460×680. Alternatives: B, a sidebar; C, two panes. Sketches.
  3. The bottom status strip goes. Connection state moves into the hero. Settings, About and Admin move into a ⋯ menu in the header on Windows and into the app menu on macOS. The version moves into About.
  4. Desktop type scale. Readex Pro at the desktop density: body 14, captions 12 in English and 13 in Arabic, against the phone's body 16. The system UI fonts (Segoe UI, and Helvetica with Geeza Pro) are dropped.
  5. App icon. A white symbol on a teal plate on both systems: a rounded square in the .ico and Apple's squircle in the .icns. It is the phone's launcher (option B), and it is also used for toasts, the installer and the window icon.
  6. Windows tray glyph. A monochrome glyph that follows the taskbar: ink on a light taskbar, white on a dark one, like Windows' own icons. It is not teal, which is 3.04:1 on the dark taskbar, and not the plate, which is soft at 16 px. This needs the app to read the taskbar theme, a small Windows-only service that serves the UI.
  7. The tray and menu-bar icon shows status. There are four shapes: available (the symbol), not available (dimmed), can't reach the server (the arch broken at its crown) and in a session (a third dot). This is an exception to the phone rule that keeps the motif out of system surfaces. The alternative is one static icon, with the state shown in the tooltip and the menu.
  8. Window frames. Standard system frames with a solid canvas, the same on Windows 10 and 11. No Mica for now: it tints the background from the wallpaper, so the AA contrast of text cannot be guaranteed. Mica stays an option for a later pass. The alternative is Mica behind the main window on Windows 11.
  9. Dialog buttons follow each system. On Windows the primary button comes first and Cancel second. On macOS Cancel comes first and the primary button sits at the trailing edge. Both mirror in Arabic. On the request window Enter never accepts, and Esc means "decide later" (the request is dismissed, as today).
  10. The request window. Accept and Reject have equal weight (the phone's decision). The consequence is stated in plain words directly above them. Ticking "always allow" renames Accept to "Accept and always allow". Turning on trust from the Contacts tab asks for confirmation. An expired request stays on screen and says so (a view-model addition).
  11. Keyboard. Ctrl/⌘ , opens Settings. Ctrl/⌘ W closes the window to the tray or menu bar. ⌘ Q on macOS and the tray's Exit on Windows quit, and ask for confirmation first while you are sharing or in a session (a UI-only addition).
  12. Wording. Add new Desktop* keys where the desktop needs different words. Edit a shared key only where both apps benefit equally (the same rule as the phone's decision 6). The full copy table comes with Phase 2.
  13. One icon set. The 14 Fluent glyphs the desktop draws today are replaced by the phone's own 24-unit icon set (2-unit stroke, round caps), shared through Josour.Brand, with the few glyphs only the desktop needs added in the same style.
  14. macOS keeps its Dock icon. Josour stays a regular app, so it has an app menu. That menu gains About, Settings and Quit through NativeMenu. The alternative is a menu-bar-only app with no Dock icon and no app menu.

What carries over from the phone

The phone's Phase 1 and 2 decisions were approved and shipped in v2.6.0 (docs/design/mobile-phase1-foundation.html, mobile-phase2-mockups.html, mobile-tokens.json). They bind the desktop. Where one does not suit a desktop it is a numbered decision above. None is changed silently.

Approved on the phoneOn the desktop
Readex Pro for Arabic and Latin, four static weights (OFL), no Noto NaskhAs is. The same four files, from one place (decision 1). It replaces Segoe UI on Windows and Helvetica with a Geeza Pro fallback on macOS (Program.cs:97-104).
Teal #0E7490 light, #5ECCE4 dark; ink neutrals; the role tableAs is: every colour role, in both themes, with the same keys (Josour.Brush.*). The desktop adds only hover, pressed, menu, tooltip and scrim (below).
Semantic success, warning, danger and info, each with its own icon shapeAs is. They replace InfoBar's hard-coded light-only hex values (Controls/InfoBar.axaml:57-89).
Logo white on dark; lock-up AR-first in Arabic, EN-first in EnglishAs is: on Login, First run and About.
The arch as the status motif; a hero may break it; never decorationAs is: the status hero (decision 2). Decision 7 asks whether the tray icon may use the broken arch.
Radius 6 / 12 / 18 / 24, the 4-px spacing scaleSame scales, used at desktop density: controls 6, cards 12, hero 18.
Type sizes 28 / 22 / 18 / 16 / 14 / 13; touch target 48Changed for the desktop (decision 4): 24 / 20 / 16 / 14 / 12-13; pointer target 32 (min 24).
HostStatus, trust confirmation, expired request, sign-out reason (view-model additions)The same additions on the desktop's own view models (Phase 2 lists them). No networking change.

The largest frame is 64 px. It feeds the exe, every window's Icon, the tray (TrayService.cs:18), the toast registration and the .icns, which publish-app.sh:94-117 upscales to 1024 px. That upscale is why the Dock icon is soft.

Strings

The desktop reads 339 strings through Strings.cs, from the resx files it shares with the phone. 101 of them are also used by the phone, so editing their value changes both apps. That is why Phase 2 tags every change new Desktop*, edit-shared or same. About 30 are no longer shown anywhere: the old hosts list (Guest*Hosts*, HostReachable and others) and the old auto-accept settings (SettingsAutoAccept*, AutoAcceptTrust*). Removing them is a follow-up.

The five shared edits the phone made in v2.6.0 already show on the desktop: From as the requester label, "seconds left to answer" for the countdown, "the person who runs your Josour server" in the account and session messages, and "this server's list of allowed sites".

The main window: three layouts

The window is opened now and then: to check that the app is ready, to ask a contact for their connection, to answer an invitation or to end a session. Most of the time Josour sits in the tray, and a request arrives in its own window. These are low-fidelity sketches. Phase 2 draws the chosen one in full.

A · Hero + tabsB · SidebarC · Two panes
Size460×680, min 400×560: a tray companion720×560: a "real" app window760×560, collapsing to A below 600 px
Status always visibleYes (hero)Only on the Status pageYes (left pane)
Matches the phoneClosely: hero, then the same two tabsNoPartly
SessionThe hero becomes the session; the tabs stayA Session pageThe left pane becomes the session
Arabic and 200% riskLow: one columnMedium: the rail mirrorsHigh: two columns of Arabic at 760 px, and a second layout to test
CostLowMediumHigh (container queries, two layouts)

Recommendation: A. The window stays small, like a tray app, and answers "can a request reach me?" before anything else. It is the layout the phone's users already know. B and C use a desktop's width but make a short visit longer: the status or the contacts are one click away instead of both being on screen.

The bottom status strip (settings, about, admin, version, connection text) is not in the right place. Its connection text repeats what the hero says, its three icon-only buttons have no names, and the strip competes with the session's buttons. Decision 3 moves its parts to where each system expects them: the ⋯ menu in the header (Windows), the app menu (macOS) and About (the version).

The Share tab's four warnings, ranked

The rank decides which warning gets the hero and which become rows in "This device". The rule is the one the phone uses: first, can a request arrive at all; then, can the other device connect; then, whether sharing still does what the host expects.

#Condition (existing view-model fact)Why this rankShown as
1Not connected to the server, for 5 s or more (!IsConnected)No request can arrive. Everything else is moot.The hero: broken arch, "Requests can't reach you", Reconnect.
2No inbound firewall rule (IsFirewallRuleMissing, Windows)A request arrives, but the session may never connect: the most confusing failure.The hero: "Needs attention", with a "How to fix" link. A row while 1 holds.
3A VPN carries outbound traffic (IsVpnWarningVisible)Sharing works, but sites see the VPN's address, which defeats the purpose without breaking anything.A warning row in "This device", with an icon, a title and one line.
4A simulated server (IsSimulatedServer)A development build. Information, not a problem.An info row at the end of "This device".

A reconnect shorter than 5 s reads as "Getting ready…" (the phone's rule). That needs the HostStatus view-model addition, which Phase 2 specifies for the desktop.

Focus, cursor, elevation

Focus

A 2 px ring in focus, 1 px outside the control and following its radius. Filled controls get a 1 px inner line in surface, so the ring reads on teal. It shows on keyboard focus only, never on a mouse click. Tab order follows reading order in both directions.

Cursor

Arrow over buttons, rows and toggles; hand only over links; I-beam in fields. That is the convention on both systems, where a hand over a button reads as "web page".

Elevation

Cards sit flat with a border (desktop density). Menus and tooltips use elevation 2, and in-window confirmation dialogs use 3 over a scrim. Windows keep the system's own shadow. Dark mode uses no shadows: a lighter surface and a border, as on the phone.

One source of truth for the identity

Constraint 4: colours are never copied into the desktop by hand. The two ways to do that, with cost and risk:

1 · Extend the generator

mobile-theme.py becomes brand-theme.py, reads one brand-tokens.json, and also writes Josour.App/Theme/Tokens.axaml, a desktop BrandGeometry.g.cs, the .ico, the .icns iconset and the tray template images. Each app keeps its own controls.

  • Cost: small. One script and one new output folder.
  • Risk to the phone: very low. Its outputs stay byte-identical (--check proves it).
  • Drawback: the lock-up, the motif and the icon controls are written twice, once in each project. The motif's states and the lock-up's language rule are identity, and two copies drift. The fonts are linked into two projects.

2 · A shared project, Josour.Brand (recommended)

A net8.0 class library referenced by Josour.App and Josour.Mobile. It holds Theme/Tokens.axaml (generated: colours for both themes, radii, space), the four Readex Pro files with OFL.txt, BrandGeometry.g.cs, and the BrandLockup, Motif and Icon controls, moved from the phone. Each app keeps its own density (a generated Theme/Metrics.axaml) and its own control themes.

  • Cost: medium. A new project in Josour.sln, the phone's three controls moved (a namespace change in its XAML and tests), and a reduced-motion setting that each head fills in.
  • Risk to the phone: low to medium. Resource keys stay identical (Josour.Brush.*), so the phone's views do not change. The Android build gains one more assembly (watch EmbedAssembliesIntoApk). Josour.Mobile.Tests and --check must stay green at the step where the phone switches.
  • Benefit: the identity lives in exactly one place: tokens, font, geometry and the components that draw them.

Recommendation: 2, done as the first step of Phase 3. Create Josour.Brand, move the phone onto it with its tests green, and only then build the desktop on it. The generator becomes scripts/brand-theme.py, the only writer of generated files. The publish scripts call its --check so that a release cannot ship stale icons.

Icon plan for each system

Every proof below is drawn by Skia, the renderer Avalonia uses, from the symbol path in 1-qantara/symbol-teal.svg, copied and never redrawn. Each size is shown at 1:1 and enlarged with no smoothing, so the pixels are visible. The light taskbar is #F3F3F3, the dark one #202020.

Windows · tray (notification area)

The tray asks for 16, 20, 24 and 32 px at 100, 125, 150 and 200% scaling. The symbol is 16.5 units tall on a 24-unit grid, so it is moved up 3 units to sit centred. Then the arch's edges, the band and the dots land on whole pixels at 16, 24 and 32 px (the band is 2, 3 and 4 px). At 20 px they fall on half pixels, which is the usual cost of that scale.

Contrast against the taskbar: teal is 4.83:1 on light but 3.04:1 on dark, where it looks dim. Monochrome is 15.7:1 and 16.3:1. The plate is legible on both, but at 16 px its symbol is 11 px wide with a 1.7 px band, and it reads as a blob beside Windows' own outline icons. That is why decision 6 recommends B. B needs the taskbar theme (SystemUsesLightTheme) and a listener for its changes.

Tray and menu-bar states (decision 7)

The two states that need action, can't reach the server and in a session, differ from the plain symbol in shape. Not available is dimmed, the usual sign of an inactive tray icon, and it is a state the person chose. The tooltip and the menu's first line always say the state in words, so none of it depends on the icon alone.

One .ico with 16, 20, 24, 32, 48, 64 and 256 px frames, generated from the symbol. It serves the exe, the taskbar button, Alt+Tab, the Start menu and Explorer, each window's title bar, the toast registration and the installer (SetupIconFile, UninstallDisplayIcon).

The app icon is not theme-aware: an .ico cannot switch with the taskbar, which is another reason it is the plate and not a bare symbol. Teal alone would fall to 3.04:1 on a dark taskbar. The plate's white symbol is 5.36:1 on teal everywhere.

macOS · app icon (.icns)

Apple's grid: a 1024 canvas with an 824 pt continuous-corner squircle at 100,100. The plate carries the template's soft shadow; the symbol never does. The symbol is 60% of the plate's width, centred on its own bounds. This replaces publish-app.sh's conversion of josour.ico (from 64 px). Phase 3 writes the full iconset from 16 to 1024 @2x, and iconutil packs it.

macOS · menu bar (template image)

A template image is black plus alpha, and the system tints it for a light or dark menu bar, for a selected item and for a menu bar over a wallpaper. That is why it cannot be the coloured .ico used today. The canvas is 18×18 pt, and the symbol is 15 pt wide, leaving room for the "in a session" dot. Avalonia's TrayIcon needs MacOSProperties.IsTemplateIcon set. Below, each state appears as the system tints it, at @2x (Retina) and @1x.

Toasts, notifications and the installer

SurfacePlan
Windows toastThe new .ico through the toast registration (DisplayName and IconUri). A request toast gets the plate as its app logo override, cropped to a circle as Windows expects. Wording follows the request window's (Phase 2). The Accept and Reject buttons stay.
macOS notificationToday these are attributed to Script Editor, and that cannot be fixed by an icon. Only a signed .app with UNUserNotificationCenter shows Josour's name and icon (ADR-0011). Recorded as a follow-up.
Installer (Inno Setup)SetupIconFile = the new .ico. The modern wizard's two images are generated as well: WizardSmallImageFile (the plate, 55×55 to 138×140 for each DPI) and WizardImageFile (the English lock-up on the canvas colour, 164×314 to 410×797). The installer is English only today.
GenerationAll of these, plus the tray PNGs and the macOS template, come from scripts/brand-theme.py (decision 1). --check fails when any of them is stale. publish-app.sh and publish-exe.ps1 run the check before packaging.

Platform conventions

One identity and each system's own manners. These are planned for Phase 3 and drawn in Phase 2.

Windows 10 and 11macOS
FrameThe standard frame. The title bar follows the light or dark theme (Avalonia sets it). Solid canvas (decision 8).The standard frame with traffic lights. Nothing is drawn in the title area, so the lights and the window title keep their place.
ThemeFollows the system while the app runs (RequestedThemeVariant="Default" and ActualThemeVariantChanged). The tray glyph follows the taskbar on Windows; the template image needs nothing.
App menuNone (not a Windows pattern). A ⋯ menu in the header: Settings, About, Admin, Sign out.NativeMenu: Josour → About Josour, Settings… (⌘,), Hide, Quit Josour (⌘Q); Window → Close (⌘W).
ShortcutsCtrl , Settings · Ctrl W close to tray · Esc cancels dialogs · Alt F4 closes to tray⌘ , Settings · ⌘ W close · ⌘ Q quit (asks while sharing) · Esc cancels
Dialog buttons[Primary] [Cancel], at the trailing edge[Cancel] [Primary], primary at the trailing edge
Request windowTopmost, not resizable, focus on the heading, no default button (Enter never accepts), Esc = decide later. Accept and Reject have equal weight in each system's order. Both are mirrored in Arabic.
Tray / menu barLeft click opens the window; right click opens the menu.A click opens the menu, as menu-bar items do. "Show Josour" is the first item.
DPIChecked at 100, 150 and 200% (headless at 2× in Phase 4). Icons come from the vector source or the right .ico frame.Retina @2x for every raster asset.
Screen readerNarrator, through Avalonia's UIA automation peersVoiceOver, through its NSAccessibility peers. Both need names on icon buttons, toggles and the hero (LiveSetting).

Follow-ups (out of scope, not done)

  • macOS notifications as Josour. They need a signed bundle and UNUserNotificationCenter (ADR-0011). Until then they show as Script Editor, with no actions.
  • About 30 unused strings (the old hosts list and the old auto-accept settings) in the shared resx. Removing them touches the phone's resx files too.
  • The Linux overlap on the Contacts tab (two elements in one grid row). It is fixed by the rebuild, but Linux is not a shipped target.
  • The web admin dashboard (favicon, header), and the screenshots in the README and docs, are to be updated to the new identity after Phase 3.
  • The installer is English only. Arabic Inno Setup messages would be a separate change.

Method notes

  • Captures: a scratch harness, outside the repo, built the real App through Program.ConfigureApp on the headless platform with Skia. It loaded each view's own XAML through Avalonia's runtime loader, with plain sample objects in place of the view models. The request window used its real view model. A headless lifetime is not a desktop lifetime, so App.Start() never ran, and nothing read or wrote ~/Library/Application Support/Josour. The real app was not launched.
  • Resource check: the same harness asked the running app for ThemeBackgroundBrush, ThemeBorderMidBrush and SystemFillColorCriticalBrush. All three are missing under FluentTheme.
  • Icon proofs: Skia rasterised the exact symbol path into RenderTargetBitmap at each pixel size, with no resampling. The macOS squircle is approximated by a superellipse (n = 4.2). Phase 3 uses Apple's continuous-corner shape.
  • Contrast: the WCAG 2.x relative-luminance ratio, computed the same way as on the phone pages.
  • Not verified on real hardware: how Windows draws the tray at each DPI, the macOS menu bar's real tint, the toast, and Narrator and VoiceOver. These are listed again for Phase 4.
